First-principles-based Machine Learning Models for Phase Behavior and Transport Properties of CO2 Reha Mathur,1, a) Maria Carolina Muniz,1, a) Shuwen Yue,1 Roberto Car,2 and Athanassios Z. Panagiotopoulos*1, b)

1)Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA 2)Department of Chemistry, Department of Physics, Program in Applied and Computational Mathematics, Princeton Institute for the Science and Technology of Materials, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA

(Dated: 18 April 2023)

ABSTRACT: In this work, we construct distinct ﬁrst-principles-based machine-learning models of CO2, reproducing the potential energy surface of the PBE-D3, BLYP-D3, SCAN and SCAN-rvv10 approximations of density functional theory. We employ the Deep Potential methodology to develop the models and consequently achieve a signiﬁcant computational eﬃciency over ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) that allows for larger system sizes and time scales to be explored. Although our models are trained only with liquid phase conﬁgurations, they are able to simulate a stable interfacial system and predict vapor-liquid equilibrium properties, in good agreement with results from the literature. Because of the computational eﬃciency of the models, we are also able to obtain transport properties, such as viscosity and diﬀusion coeﬃ- cients. We ﬁnd that the SCAN-based model presents a temperature shift in the position of the critical point, while the SCAN-rvv10-based model shows improvement but still exhibits a temperature shift that remains approximately constant for all properties investigated in this work. We ﬁnd that the BLYP-D3-based model generally performs better for liquid phase and vapor-liquid equilibrium properties, but the PBE-D3-based model is better suited for predicting transport properties.

## I. INTRODUCTION

High levels of atmospheric CO2 are the primary factor in the ongoing global temperature rise, leading to severe environmental consequences such as rising sea levels and ocean acidiﬁcation.1–4 Carbon capture and sequestration has been proposed as a method to reduce emissions to the atmosphere without compromising energy production. In this approach, the emitted CO2 is captured at its source, transported through a pipeline either as a gas or liquid, and stored underground in porous geologic formations such as deep saline aquifers.5–7 Experimentally studying these processes involves recreating the subsurface conditions of these geologic reservoirs, which can be challenging due to the high temperature, pressure and salinity conditions.8,9 In view of this, molecular simulations can provide detailed insights of these processes, by allowing the calculation of a variety of structural, thermodynamic and transport properties of CO2 under a wide range of conditions. Empirical force ﬁelds provide an eﬃcient way to simulate CO2 molecules, usually consisting of simple functional forms with parameters obtained by ﬁtting speciﬁc experimental data. When applied to conditions close to the ones used in their parameterization, these models can indeed be successful, which explains their widespread use. As an example, models such as EPM210 and TraPPE11,

parameterized to vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) experimental data, perform reasonably well for predicting the critical point and coexistence densities.10,12–16 However, due to the empirical nature of these models, they often lack in transferability and may fail when predicting other properties not targeted during model parameterization. For the case of EPM2 and TraPPE, these models fall short in representing two-phase coexistence properties when applied to mixtures of CO2 and water.17,18Most empirical models do not account for polarizability and many-body eﬀects and may depend on implicit error cancellation in describing physical interactions.17,18 Improving upon these empirical models and extending their applicability to mixtures is not straightforward. For instance, the performance on water/CO2 would depend also on the compatibility with the chosen water model and its accuracy for pure water. Factors such as inclusion of many-body eﬀects or polarizability have been considered to increase accuracy of empirical models17,19,20, but that alone might not lead to the desired result. For example, for CO2, a linear and symmetric molecule with zero dipole moment, incorporating polarizability may not be enough to achieve signiﬁcant improvements. Polarizability eﬀects were shown to present a bigger impact in mixtures with polar molecules such as water.20,21

Ideally, to represent interactions in CO2 over a broad range of thermodynamic states, ab initio methods can be used to obtain points on the potential energy surface. Saharay et al. applied density functional theory (DFT) with the Perdew-Burke-Enzerhof (PBE) functional and ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to predict the structure, the dynamics and vibrational modes

of supercritical CO2 in good agreement with experimental results.22,23 Balasubramian et al. later revised these calculations by including an empirical vdW correction to the interaction energy to account for the dispersion forces present in CO2.24 They found signiﬁcant changes in the pair correlation functions, emphasizing the importance of including dispersion corrections into CO2 force ﬁelds.24

Goel et al.25 assessed the accuracy of various functionals in predicting the vapor-liquid equilibrium of CO2 and concluded that PBE and BLYP with D3 dispersion correction perform reasonably well in predicting VLE properties and molecular structure properties. However, the high computational expense associated with such calculations constrains AIMD simulations to timescales of a few hundred picoseconds and system sizes of fewer than a hundred atoms, limiting their applicability. Alternatively, several models have been constructed by parameterizing force ﬁelds to ab initio data. Bukowski et al. developed the many-body symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT),26 which accurately predicts second virial coeﬃcients. Bock et al. also predicted second virial coeﬃcients in excellent agreement with experimental results by using a four-dimensional potential energy surface ﬁtted to second-order Møller-Plesset perturbation (MP2) theory calculations.27 However, for bulk thermodynamic properties such as VLE, Bratschi et al. has shown that these two models fall short.28 To improve upon these results, Yu et al. developed a physically motivated force ﬁeld ﬁtted to the SAPT energy calculations, which produced accurate predictions of the VLE, density, isobaric heat capacity and diﬀusion of CO2. However, the accuracy of the model relied on empirically scaling the dispersion coeﬃcients parameterized from the SAPT calculations.29 Their subsequent revision to incorporate three-body eﬀects reduced but it did not completely eliminate the need for a scaling factor. Higgoda et al. also generated a force-ﬁeld parameterized to ab initio data by developing a model ﬁt to pair potentials calculated at the CCSD(T) level of theory, yielding improved predictions of the self-diﬀusion coeﬃcient and viscosity relative to other common force ﬁelds, though it is unclear how this model performs for VLE properties.30 Yue et al.31 developed a data-driven many-body model by ﬁtting a model to large sets of one-body and two-body energies calculated with the CCSD(T) level of theory. The model’s predicted second virial coeﬃcients agreed well with experimental results but for the VLE properties, scaling was needed to attain reasonable agreement with experimental results. In order to overcome the computational drawbacks of these existing models and to improve model accuracy and transferability, machine learning (ML) techniques can be applied to construct the potential energy surface and match the accuracy of ab initio methods eﬃ- ciently. Because of their data-driven nature, applicability can be extended to diﬀerent systems and conditions, as long as the training sets selected to develop these models are representative. In this work, we utilize the Deep

Potential (DP) scheme to develop neural-network-based potentials for CO2.32,33 Through this scheme, in order to represent the potential energy surface, a deep neural network is trained to a set of reference energies and atomic forces generated from ﬁrst-principles DFT calculations. The resulting potential energy surface can then be used to perform “deep potential molecular dynamics” (DPMD)33 simulations eﬃciently. DP models trained upon DFT calculations have been shown to achieve accuracies comparable to the reference DFT data for a variety of systems.34–38 Furthermore as a testament to their computational eﬃciency, such models have been used to simulate millions of atoms on timescales of tens of nanoseconds.39

In this work, ML models were obtained for CO2 based on four diﬀerent reference DFT exchange-correlation functionals: the Perdew-Burke-Enzerhof (PBE)40 and the Becke-Lee-Yang-Parr (BLYP),41 both with the D3 dispersion correction,42 the strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN) functional, and SCANrvv10, including long-range vdW interactions from the revised Vydrov-Voorhis (rVV10) nonlocal correlation functional.43 Using these models, bulk liquid densities were ﬁrst calculated in isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble simulations. Direct-coexistence molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were also performed to assess their accuracy in reproducing vapor-liquid equilibrium properties such as coexistence densities, interfacial tension, and vapor pressures. Finally, the self-diﬀusion coef- ﬁcient and viscosity of CO2 were also obtained with the three models. The article is organized as follows. In section II, we discuss the data preparation, construction of the DP models and our simulation and analysis methodologies. In section III, we analyze and assess the results obtained from our models to understand the overall accuracy of these density functionals and DP implementation. Section IV includes our conclusions and potential future investigations.

## II. METHODS

## A. Development of DP models

All models were constructed following the DP methodology.32 For every conﬁguration in the training set, the positions of each atom and its neighbors within a cutoﬀrc were converted to a set of "descriptors" that preserve translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries. To construct the descriptors, a local environment frame is considered for each atom, deﬁned by the speciﬁed cutoﬀradius. A weighting function is also applied, gradually reducing the weight of neighbors that are further way from the center atom and thus removing the discontinuity brought by the cutoﬀradius. The atomic coordinates of each atom and the neighbors within the frame are processed into neural network descriptors that


<!-- Page 3 -->


3

contain angular and radial information and are invariant for permutations of atoms of the same chemical species, providing a symmetry-preserving representation of the local environment of each atom.33,44 For all models, rc was chosen to be 6 Å. The descriptors then serve as inputs to a deep neural network with three hidden layers each containing 90 neurons to output the atomic energies. The total energy of a given conﬁguration is given by the sum of the individual atomic energies. The atomic forces were obtained by taking the gradient of the energy. The parameters of the neural network are obtained by minimizing the loss function (L), deﬁned as the sum of the square errors of the system energy (∆E) and atomic forces (∆Fi) normalized by the number of atoms. The prefactors pe and pf are tunable parameters, varying during the optimization process.

Four DP models were constructed based on density functional theory (DFT). The ﬁrst two were based on the Perdew-Burke-Enzerhof (PBE) functional40 and the Becke-Lee-Yang-Parr (BLYP) functional41 respectively, both with dispersion correction D3 applied42. The other two were based on the strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN) functional45 and a version of SCAN with long-range van der Waals interactions, SCAN-rvv1043. For the construction of the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based models, the training data were labeled through single point calculations performed with the CP2K46 quantum chemistry software package. For both models, the Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) pseudopotential47 was used to model the core electrons in the C and O atoms. An energy cutoﬀof 600 Ry for the electron density was used. For the SCANand SCAN-rvv10-based models, the quantum chemistry software package Quantum Espresso48 was used for the single point calculations. Troullier-Martins (TM) pseudopotentials49 were used, with energy cutoﬀs for the Kohn-Sham orbitals of 150 Ry and 240 Ry for the SCAN and SCAN-RVV10-based models, respectively. Dimer potential energy curves for all four DFT methods can be found in the Supporting Information. For all models, conﬁgurations forming the initial training set were obtained from classical MD simulations of bulk liquid states at T=220-300K and P=100 bar for a system of 64 molecules in the isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble, with the TraPPE11 force ﬁeld. Subsequently, these conﬁgurations were labeled through single point calculations using the selected DFT method. Additional conﬁgurations were added to the training set through the active learning scheme DPGEN50 to adequately sample the conﬁgurational phase space. In total, 2,414 and 3,800 conﬁgurations were used to train the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based models, respectively. For the SCAN and SCAN-rVV10-based models, the same 1,301 conﬁgurations were used to construct each training set.

## B. Ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulations

We validated the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based models by running ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations with the respective DFT functionals and pseudopotentials. The CP2K software package46 was used and simulations with a system of 64 CO2 molecules at P=100 bar and T=220-280K were run for 40-50ps. The same energy cutoﬀof 600 Ry was applied. For these calculations, we used 4 Intel Skylake nodes with 2.4 GHz, 128 CPU cores and achieved a performance of approximately 8.3 ps/day for a 64-molecule system. Pair correlation functions obtained from the AIMD simulations are reported in Supporting Information and match well literature data as well as correlation functions obtained from the DP models for the corresponding DFT methods.

## C. Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics Simulations

The LAMMPS package51 with the DeePMD-kit plugin32 was used for all simulations performed with the constructed DP models. For all MD simulations with DP models, a timestep of 0.5 fs was used. Using a single Xeon Broadwell E5-2680 v4 node, with 2.4 GHz and one 1328 MHz NVIDIA P100 GPU, 28 Intel Broadwell e5-2680v4 CPU cores, we were able to simulate a 64-molecule system with a speed of 4.5ns/day.

## 1. Bulk Densities

To calculate liquid densities using the constructed DP models, NPT simulations at P=100 bar and T=220-280K were performed with a system of 512 CO2 molecules. A stochastic velocity-rescale thermostat with a relaxation time of 0.5 ps and 0.05 ps was used to maintain the pressure and temperature, respectively. The simulations were run for 4-5 ns with at least 2 ns of equilibration.

## 2. Vapor-liquid equilibrium

Direct coexistence simulations were performed to obtain vapor-liquid equilibrium properties of CO2. A vapor-liquid interfacial system was generated by expanding an equilibrated liquid box of CO2 along the zdimension to produce a liquid slab in the x-y plane. In the canonical ensemble, simulations were performed with 1024 molecules and the Nosé-Hoover thermostat was applied for temperature control. The interfacial system was equilibrated for at least 1ns and sampled for at least 4ns. The box size was 31 x 31 x 250 Å3 for the PBE-D3 and SCAN-rvv10-based DP models and 26 x 26 x 250 Å3 for the BLYP-D3-based DP model. The distinct box sizes were chosen so as to accommodate suﬃciently large liquid and vapor slabs.

## 3. Transport Properties

The Einstein relationship was used to compute selfdiﬀusion coeﬃcients (D) using the DP models. A condensed phase box at T=220-300 K with 512 molecules was ﬁrst equilibrated through an NPT simulation using the Nose-Hoover thermostat and barostat for temperature and pressure control, respectively. Using conﬁgurations with densities close to the average density obtained from the NPT simulations, NV T simulations were run for at least 1.5ns and the mean squared displacements of the C atoms were obtained. The self-diﬀusion coeﬃ- cient was calculated from the slope of the mean-squared displacement versus time. The shear viscosities were calculated using the Green- Kubo relation:

where V is the volume of the simulation box and Pαβ is the oﬀ-diagonal element of the pressure tensor. The autocorrelation functions of the Pxy, Pyz, Pzx were averaged to improve statistics. At the obtained liquid densities for T=220-280K, simulations in the canonical ensemble were run for 1.5ns to equilibrate a liquid box of 512 molecules using the Nose-Hoover thermostat. Conﬁgurations with energies close to the equilibrium were selected to serve as starting points for simulations in the microcanonical ensemble (NV E). The NV E simulations for viscosity calculation were run for 4-5ns. The upper time limit for the Green-Kubo integral was chosen to be 500 ps based upon the speed of the decay of the autocorrelation function.

## III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Results for the bulk liquid densities at P = 1000 bar as a function of temperature for each DP model are compared to experimental data in Fig. 1. Tabulated data and statistical uncertainties for this and subsequent ﬁgures can be found in the article’s Supporting Information. We found that on one hand, the DP SCAN model underestimates densities by approximately 10%, while the DP SCAN-rvv10 model, on the other hand, overestimates them by approximately 8%. Densities from the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based DP models agree well


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

with the corresponding AIMD results. In agreement with a prior study,25 while the PBE-D3 functional underpredicts the bulk liquid densities, the BLYP-D3 functional slightly overpredicts them. Furthermore, the PBE-D3- based model results are comparable to the ones by the SCAN-based model. Overall, for the bulk liquid phase, we ﬁnd that BLYP-D3 functional is better suited for describing the equation-of-state, providing a good description of van der Waals interactions for this condensed phase. These observations of the relative performance of the four diﬀerent DFT methods for equation-of-state data are consistent with the underlying dimer potential energy curves shown in Supplementary Information. Speciﬁcally, the SCAN-rvv10 method provides a deeper potential well, while the SCAN method has a faster decay of the attractions at longer distances relative to PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3. It should be pointed out that the divergences in liquid density values, specially between SCAN and SCAN-rvv10 results, can be due to several sources. For one, the distinct representation of long-range dispersion should be taken into consideration. While SCAN only oﬀers a portion of intermediate-range dispersion interactions representation, SCAN-rvv10 includes long-range vdW interactions. The D3 and rvv10 can be viewed as two complementary approaches to describe long-range interactions in real systems. While rvv10 can be seen as a conceptually simpler approach, both rvv10 and D3 require empirical parts in their representations and have yielded similar results for a study on cluster interactions55. More details about dispersion correction approaches can be found in reviews, such as Ref. 56. Furthermore, the short-range nature of the machine learning models should be contemplated here. While the reference DFT methods might include dispersion corrections, the DP models only consider a local representation within a pre-deﬁned cutoﬀradius. This means that dispersion corrections are only implicitly taken into account in these models, which might lead to discrepancies between the interactions predicted by DP models and the DFT reference methods. As an additional remark on the representation of the bulk liquid phase, we make a note that we have also calculated liquid densities at a lower pressure, that of P = 100 bar. At this lower pressure, we found that DP SCAN fails to reproduce experimental densities, greatly underestimating them, while the other models show behavior similar to that at P = 1000 bar. These conditions are in the general vicinity of the critical point for CO2, making the liquid highly compressible. These results can be found in the Supplementary Information. Given the inadequate description of the liquid phase provided by the SCAN-based model at P = 100 bar, we make use only of the PBE-D3, BLYP-D3 and SCANrvv10 based models in the remainder of this work for the calculations of properties along the vapor-liquid coexistence curve. Speciﬁcally, we evaluated the performance of the DP models for the vapor-liquid equilibrium properties of CO2. Through direct coexistence MD simulations,

we calculated vapor and liquid coexistence densities, surface tensions and saturation vapor pressures. For the PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based DP models, we were also able to compare our results to the AIMD simulations of Goel et al.25

Even though no interfacial snpashots were added into the training set of the models, all three DP models were able to simulate a stable interfacial system with a clear separation between the vapor and liquid phases as shown by Fig. 2. For the DPMD BLYP-D3 simulations, when T > 270K, the results from the ﬁt become less representative since the interface starts to lose deﬁnition signaling proximity to the critical point. Results from both PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based DP models agree well with AIMD results from Goel et al. The discrepancies shown between the AIMD and DPMD results are likely due to the longer simulation times and greater system sizes used in our DPMD simulations. Additionally, the shortrange nature of DP models, lacking an explicit inclusion of long-range dispersion interactions may also contribute to these discrepancies. However, these results still corroborate that PBE-D3 underpredicts coexistence liquid densities while BLYP-D3 slightly overpredicts them. The same is true for vapor coexistence densities, with PBE- D3 underestimating and BLYP-D3 slightly overestimating experimental results. The SCAN-rvv10-based DP model in turn underpredicts coexistence vapor densities and overpredicts even more coexistence liquid densities when compared to BLYP-based DP model, in alignment with the liquid densities results discussed earlier in this section. From the direct coexistence simulations with the PBE- D3 and BLYP-D3-based DP models, we estimated the critical temperatures and densities using Eqs. 3 and 4. For DP PBE-D3 we found the critical temperature to be 322±5 K and critical density to be 0.43±0.01 g/cm3. For DP BLYP-D3 we obtained a critical temperature 291±8

K and density of 0.52±0.02 g/cm3, respectively. These results are within statistical uncertainties from the ones reported by Goel et al25 for a signiﬁcantly smaller system size, namely T=328±40 K, ρ=0.4±0.1 g/cm3 for PBE-D3 and T= 319±60 K and ρ=0.5±0.2 g/cm3 for BLYP-D3. The lower uncertainties of our results are due to the longer simulation time scales of the DPMD simulations. From experimental data, the critical temperature and density of CO2 are 304.12 K and 0.467 g/cm3, respectively. In summary, we found that DP PBE-D3 model overpredicts the critical temperature and underpredicts the critical density. Contrariwise, the DP BLYP- D3 model slightly underpredicts the critical temperature and overpredicts the critical density. Since Eqs. 3 and 4 can only be used with coexistence densities close to the critical point, we were not able to execute this calculation with the obtained coexistence values for DP SCANrvv10. Nevertheless, our results indicate that SCANrvv10 signiﬁcantly overpredicts the critical temperature. In addition, we evaluated the vapor-liquid surface tension γ and the saturation vapor pressure Psat results for each model, obtained through the direct coexistence simulations. Fig. 3 shows that the experimental values for surface tension are within the uncertainties of the results for both PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3-based DP models and lower than results with the SCAN-based model. Ab initio calculations have not been previously performed for the surface tension of CO2 using any of the three functionals. For the vapor pressures shown in Fig. 4, in agreement with the vapor coexistence densities results, the DP BLYP-D3 model consistently overpredicts experimental results whereas the DP PBE-D3 and DP SCAN-rvv10 models underpredict experimental results. It is worth mentioning that vapor saturation pressures are directly related to the chemical potential of CO2. This means that these results are a consequence of how well interaction energies are predicted by the model. Furthermore, the lack of explicit long-range dispersion interactions beyond the speciﬁed cutoﬀshould also aﬀect these results, given that these interactions are particularly relevant in the vapor phase. Another factor that could contribute to small discrepancies in vapor-liquid equilibrium properties is the absence of interfacial snapshots in the training sets used to develop the models. This could lead to deviations in interfacial structure and forces predicted by the DP models, when compared to the corresponding DFT reference methods. Finally, we obtain two transport properties of CO2, speciﬁcally self-diﬀusion coeﬃcient and viscosity. Fig. 5 indicates that the diﬀusion coeﬃcients predicted by both the DP PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3 models are close to the experimental results, with the PBE-D3-based model showing a better agreement, especially at lower temperatures. The DP SCAN-rvv10 model signiﬁcantly underpredicts the self-diﬀusion coeﬃcients results, when compared to DP BLYP-D3 results. ## IV. CONCLUSIONS

In this work, four distinct DP models ﬁt to the PBE- D3, BLYP-D3, SCAN and SCAN-rvv10 approximations of DFT were constructed for CO2, enabling eﬃcient simulations at ab initio-level accuracy. The PBE-D3 and BLYP-D3 DP models were validated through comparisons with AIMD simulations of both the bulk liquid phase and vapor-liquid equilibrium. Vapor-liquid surface tensions, not previously available from AIMD simulations, were also obtained using these models. DPMD represents a signiﬁcant computational speed enhancement when compared to AIMD, achieving simulation time scales of nanoseconds per wall-clock-day on a single computing node instead of only a few picoseconds

for AIMD. The longer sampling enabled by the eﬃciency of the DP models also allowed calculations of transport properties – speciﬁcally viscosities and diﬀusion coeﬃ- cients. Both BLYP-D3 and PBE-D3-based DP models are in good agreement with AIMD simulations using the corresponding functional, indicating that the models faithfully represent their underlying potential energy function. The small discrepancies observed are likely due to diﬀerent system sizes and time lengths used in DPMD and AIMD simulations, although the lack of explicit longrange dispersion representation in DP models might also contribute to these diﬀerences. For DP SCAN, our results show that it greatly underpredicts densities at the conditions studied, at which the ﬂuid phase is quite compressible. The DP SCANrvv10 model shows signiﬁcant improvement in comparison to DP SCAN, but our results show that SCAN-rvv10 result in stronger interactions, eﬀectively corresponding to a shift in temperature for all properties examined in this work, when compared to experimental results. This suggests that including the long-range van der Waals interactions is important for this system when using the SCAN functional. In closing, our results attest to the DPMD methodology’s eﬃciency and ability to accurately represent the potential energy surface of the DFT exchange-correlation functionals used in this work. Considering that the training data consisted on liquid simulations only, the DP models developed in this work have also shown to be transferable to vapor-liquid equilibrium conditions. Given the limitations of many current models to accurately represent mixtures of CO2 with water, it would be of great interest to test these models in this capacity in future work, as a further evaluation of their transferability. In addition, given the short-range nature of the DP models, the eﬀects of explicitly taking into account dispersion corrections into these models could lead to further improvements and hence be an interesting avenue for future work.
